culminate

KUL-muh-nayt -- from Latin culmen ('summit, top'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To culminate is to reach the highest point or crowning final result of a gradual process.

Months of rehearsal would culminate in a single, sold-out performance on opening night.

Example

Years of quiet research would eventually culminate in a single breakthrough discovery that changed the entire field.

Notice the buildup -- years of small, gradual steps, all pointing toward one final, decisive moment. Culminate always describes that kind of climb toward a peak, not a sudden or random event.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

crest: To crest is to reach the very top and start to come down -- a flood crests, a wave of excitement crests -- with the falling-off built into the word. To culminate is to arrive: a long climb ends at its final result rather than tipping over a top.

crown: To crown is to set the finishing glory on top of something, the way one late victory crowned a whole season. Crown looks at the single honor placed on top; culminate looks at the slow climb that finally reaches it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

begin: to start something from the very beginning

originate: to come into existence at the very start of something

Where it sits · how fully the buildup pays off — peak → culminate → climax

peak vs. culminate: Peak is weaker than culminate: ticket sales can peak and then simply drop off, while to culminate means a whole gradual process builds to its final, crowning result.

climax vs. culminate: Climax is more intense than culminate: a project can culminate in a quiet final report, but a trilogy climaxes in a single, jaw-dropping burst of maximum drama.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — -culmin-

root — -culmin-: summit, top (Latin (culmen))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin culmen meant 'summit, top,' and the suffix -ate forms the verb. When something culminates, it climbs to its own highest point -- the final peak of a long process.

Use the root in a new word: culmination

Use the root in a new word: culmination: The gold medal was the culmination of fifteen years of early mornings at the pool.

Root Check

Word Choice

Culminate almost always appears with the preposition 'in' -- a process culminates in some final result. It describes a gradual buildup toward a peak, not a sudden event.
